name: Adrenosterone (11-keto-androstenedione)
lead: Adrenosterone, also called 11-ketoandrostenedione, 11-oxoandrostenedione or Reichstein's substance G, is a steroid made in the adrenal glands. Tadeus Reichstein first isolated it from the adrenal cortex in 1936.[1] It has very weak androgenic activity on its own and is an intermediate and prohormone of 11-ketotestosterone.[1]

Since about 2007 it has been sold as a dietary supplement (often under the name 11-OXO) marketed for fat loss and muscle gain. Proponents attribute this to inhibition of 11β-HSD1, the enzyme that converts cortisone to cortisol, which would reduce cortisol activity; Wikipedia presents this as a proposed mechanism.[1]

No human clinical trial of adrenosterone supplements for body composition was found. Published work covers analytical detection for doping control and the role of 11-oxygenated androgens in conditions such as polycystic ovary syndrome.[1][2][3]

paras: It occurs in trace amounts in humans and most mammals and in larger amounts in fish.[1] It is thought to act as a competitive, selective inhibitor of 11β-HSD1, an enzyme that regenerates cortisol from cortisone, though this is described as a proposed mechanism rather than an established one.[1]
Analytical work has characterised its metabolism, including fungal biotransformation, and multi-class steroid assays include related adrenal steroids.[4][5]

Wikipedia reports that it has been sold as a supplement since 2007 for fat loss and muscle gain, with the marketing rationale based on blocking cortisol activation to limit muscle breakdown.[1] Doping-control researchers have published criteria for detecting its use.[1] It also serves as a synthesis intermediate for other steroids such as fluoxymesterone.[1]

No studies found for its use as a fat-loss or muscle supplement. Registered trials (status unknown) are examining 11-oxygenated androgens, a class that includes this compound, in women with polycystic ovary syndrome, in relation to skeletal muscle insulin sensitivity and metabolic dysfunction.[2][3]

timeline.event: Isolated from the adrenal cortex by Tadeus Reichstein.[1]
Begins to be sold as a dietary supplement for fat loss and muscle gain.[1]

card.summary: An adrenal steroid sold as '11-OXO' for fat loss via cortisol blocking; the pitch rests on a proposed mechanism with no supplement trials.
card.note: Doping-control methods exist to detect its use.

quick.overview:
Adrenosterone is a natural adrenal steroid that has been sold since about 2007 as a fat-loss and muscle supplement.

The sources reviewed contain no human trial testing it for that purpose.
quick.mechanism: It is proposed to inhibit 11β-HSD1, the enzyme that makes cortisol from cortisone, and it is a precursor to 11-ketotestosterone. Its direct androgen activity is described as extremely weak.
quick.risks: No supplement safety data from trials were found. Its legal status is not addressed in the sources reviewed, and anti-doping labs have developed ways to detect it.
